Automation Foundations: Finding the Work and Choosing the Platform

Before you build anything, you learn to spot which tasks are worth automating and to measure the time they cost. You then learn the shared language of Zapier and Make, and how each platform counts usage so you can predict cost before a client asks.
The repeat-task audit: finding work worth automating and measuring the hours

Automation tools do one thing very well: they move information from one app to another and act on it, the same way every time, without someone pressing buttons. Zapier and Make are two of the best known of these tools. They are not magic. If the work is messy, unclear or done differently each time, automation will copy the mess faster. So the first skill of an automation specialist is not building. It is **seeing** the work clearly.
A woman beside a large clock planning her tasks
An audit turns 'we are always busy' into a list of tasks with minutes attached.
What makes a task a good automation candidate
A task is a strong candidate when it passes four tests. Learn these by heart, because you will use them in every client conversation.
**It repeats.** It happens many times a week, not twice a year.
**It follows clear rules.** You can write it as 'when X happens, do Y'. If the rule is 'it depends on how I feel', it is not ready.

**The data is already digital.** The information starts in an app: a Google Form, a spreadsheet, an email, an online store. Paper records must be typed first, and that typing is not something Zapier or Make can do for you.
**Mistakes cost something.** A missed follow-up loses a sale. A wrong amount copied into an invoice causes a dispute. The more a mistake costs, the more a reliable automation is worth.

Tasks that need judgement, such as deciding whether to give a customer a refund, approving a loan, or replying to an angry complaint, should keep a person in charge. Automation can still help by collecting the facts and alerting the right person, but the decision stays human.

Ask the person who does the work to keep a simple log for one normal week. A sheet with five columns is enough: task, how often, minutes each time, which apps are involved, and what goes wrong. Do not rely on memory. People usually forget the small, boring tasks, and those small tasks are often the best ones to automate.

Turning minutes into money

Owners respond to hours and naira, not to the word 'automation'. Multiply times per week by minutes each, then multiply by four for a rough month. Divide by 60 for hours. If you know what an hour of staff time costs the business, multiply again. Use the business's own figure, and say clearly that the result is an estimate.
Worked example: auditing a small catering business
For example, Funmi runs a catering business in Ibadan. Customers order through a Google Form, and her assistant does the follow-up work by hand. The assistant logged one week using the table above.
Copying orders: 25 orders × 3 minutes = 75 minutes a week.
Confirmation emails: 25 × 2 minutes = 50 minutes a week.
Friday summary: 1 × 40 minutes = 40 minutes a week.
Total manual time: 75 + 50 + 40 = 165 minutes, which is 2.75 hours a week.
The first two tasks are frequent and rule-based, so they score highest. Together they take 75 + 50 = 125 minutes a week, about 125 × 4 = 500 minutes, or roughly 8.3 hours, in a four-week month.
Funmi values her assistant's time at about ₦1,500 an hour (her own approximate figure). 8.33 hours × ₦1,500 is about ₦12,500 a month of time freed.

Funmi now has a clear first target: automate the order copy and the confirmation email, worth roughly 8 hours and about ₦12,500 of staff time a month. The Friday summary comes later, once the order data is clean.
Do not inflate the savings

An automation rarely removes every minute. Someone still checks the sheet, fixes the odd failed run and answers questions. When you present savings, round down, call them estimates, and show your working so the owner can check it.
Hidden costs of doing it by hand

Time is only part of the picture. Manual copying also creates **errors**, **delays** and **dependence on one person**. When the assistant is sick, orders pile up. Write these down in the 'what goes wrong' column, because they often matter more to the owner than the minutes. A late confirmation can make a customer think her payment was lost.

Finally, look for the **trigger moment** in each task: the exact event that starts the work. 'A new form response arrives' is a clear trigger. 'When I remember' is not. If you cannot name the trigger, the task is not ready to automate yet, and your job is to help the business define it.

Translate between Zapier and Make vocabulary

Zapier and Make look different on screen, but underneath they follow the same idea. Something happens in one app, the platform notices it, picks up the data that came with it, and uses that data to do something in another app. Once you understand this shape, you can learn any automation tool quickly, including newer ones such as n8n or Power Automate.
Two devices passing data between them
Every automation is a trigger handing data to one or more actions.
Triggers, actions and searches
A **trigger** is the event that starts the automation: a new form response, a new row in a sheet, a new paid order, a new email with an attachment. Each automation has one trigger.
An **action** is something the platform does in response: create a row, send an email, post a message, create a contact.
A **search** step looks for existing data, for example 'find the customer in the sheet whose phone number matches'. It is how you avoid creating duplicates.

In Zapier the whole automation is called a **Zap**, and each part is a **step**. In Make it is called a **scenario**, and each part is a **module**. Make draws modules as circles joined by lines on a canvas, which helps when the workflow branches.

Polling triggers and instant triggers

Most triggers are **polling** triggers. The platform asks the app at intervals, 'anything new?'. On Zapier's free plan the polling interval is 15 minutes at the time of writing, and Make's free plan allows scheduled runs at most every 15 minutes. So an automation built on a polling trigger is not instant: a form filled at 10:01 may be processed at 10:15.

**Instant** triggers work the other way round: the app sends the data to the platform the moment the event happens. Many of these use a **webhook**, which is simply a web address that receives data. If a customer needs an immediate reply, check whether the app offers an instant trigger, and tell the client honestly about any delay.

Data mapping: the heart of the work

When the trigger fires, it brings **fields**: name, phone, quantity, date. In each action you **map** these fields into the right boxes. You do not type 'Amaka' into the email; you insert the 'Name' field from the trigger, so every run uses that run's own name. Typing a fixed value where a field should go is the most common beginner mistake. The automation then sends every customer the same name or amount.

Mapping also means checking the **format**. A date may arrive as 2026-10-05 while the client's sheet expects 05/10/2026. A phone number may arrive as 0803 123 4567 while a messaging tool needs +2348031234567 (drop the first 0 and add +234). Both platforms have tools for reshaping data: Zapier has **Formatter by Zapier**, and Make has built-in functions you type into a field.
Worked example: mapping a training registration

For example, Zainab runs short Excel trainings in Kano. A Google Form collects registrations into a sheet with columns Full name, Phone, Email, Session date and Amount paid. She wants a confirmation email for each new registration.
Trigger: Google Sheets, new spreadsheet row, on the form's response sheet.
Action: Gmail, send email. 'To' is mapped to the Email field, not typed.
Subject: 'Your seat is confirmed for ' + the Session date field.
Body: 'Dear ' + Full name + ', we have received ₦' + Amount paid + '. See you on ' + Session date + '.'
She tests with a sample row: Full name Hauwa, Session date 12 October, Amount paid 10,000.
The test email reads 'Dear Hauwa, we have received ₦10,000. See you on 12 October.' Because every value is mapped, the next registration will get its own name, date and amount automatically.
Bundles: one run, many items

Make uses the word **bundle** for one package of data, such as one new row. Make's documentation explains that a trigger can return several bundles at once, and the modules after it run once for each bundle. If a scheduled check finds five new rows, the next module runs five times. This matters for cost, because each module run is an operation, and it matters for design, because sometimes you want one summary instead of five separate messages. You will use this in Module 2.

Clients will ask two questions early: 'Which tool should we use?' and 'What will it cost every month?'. You answer both by understanding how each platform **counts usage**. The two count differently, and a design that is cheap on one can be expensive on the other.
Two charts compared side by side
Compare the platforms on the client's real numbers, not on reputation.
How Zapier counts tasks

Zapier's help centre defines a task as any **successful action** that runs. Triggers never use tasks. Filter and Paths steps do not use tasks, and neither do utility steps such as Formatter, Delay and Storage. Steps that error or halt do not count. Zapier's own example: a Zap with a trigger and two actions uses two tasks per run, so ten runs use 20 tasks.
How Make counts credits

Make's documentation describes an **operation** as a single module run that processes data or **checks for new data**. By default one operation equals one credit. Two consequences follow. First, a scheduled trigger uses usage every time it checks, even on quiet days, so the schedule you choose changes the bill. Second, later modules run once per bundle, so ten new rows mean ten runs of each module after the trigger. Make states that router and error handler modules do not consume credits.

Worked example: the same workflow on both platforms

For example, a clinic administrator, Ifeoma, expects about 120 appointment requests a month from a form. Each request should add a row to a sheet and send an email. (No health details are collected in the form, only name, phone and preferred day.)
Zapier: trigger + 2 actions = 2 tasks per run. 120 runs × 2 = 240 tasks a month. That is more than the free 100, and a three-step Zap also needs a paid plan.
Make, checking every 15 minutes: 4 checks an hour × 24 hours × 30 days = 2,880 trigger operations, plus 120 × 2 = 240 for the actions. Far above 1,000.
Make, checking every hour: 24 × 30 = 720 checks + 240 = 960 credits. Just under 1,000, with almost no room for growth.
Make, checking every 2 hours: 12 × 30 = 360 checks + 240 = 600 credits, with room to spare.
If Ifeoma can accept replies within two hours, Make's free allowance covers this workflow. If she needs replies within minutes, either platform will need a paid plan, and the proposal must say so.

Designing to keep usage low

Good design saves money on both platforms. In Zapier, put a Filter as early as possible, so runs that should not continue stop before any action uses a task. In Make, choose the slowest schedule the client can live with, use aggregators when one message can replace many, and avoid modules that only pass data along without doing work. On both, plan for growth: if a design uses 90 per cent of an allowance in a quiet month, it will run out in a busy one. A sensible habit is to estimate usage for the busiest month of the year, such as resumption week for a school or December for a caterer, and choose the plan from that figure.
Other things to check before choosing
**Is the client's app supported?** Search the app directories on zapier.com and make.com. If an app is missing, ask whether it can send emails or webhooks, or export to Google Sheets.
**Who will maintain it?** A busy shop owner may prefer Zapier's linear editor. A team with someone technical may prefer Make's visual canvas.
**Premium apps.** Some connectors are reserved for paid plans. Check before promising.
The market for this skill

Many Nigerian and African small businesses run on Google Forms, Google Sheets, Gmail, WhatsApp and payment platforms such as Paystack, and much of the follow-up work between these tools is done by hand. That is the local opportunity: practical builds that save hours for schools, caterers, training centres, event planners and NGOs. The work is done in the browser, so remote clients abroad are also reachable once you have proof of results.

Be realistic. Clients do not buy 'automation'. They buy fewer missed orders, faster replies and cleaner records. Your audit numbers from Lesson 1 and a cost estimate like the one above are what win the work, and you will build both into proposals in Module 3.

In this lesson you build a real, useful automation on Zapier's free plan: every time someone submits a Google Form, they receive a confirmation email. It uses only two steps, one trigger and one action, so it fits the free plan's two-step limit at the time of writing. You need a Google account, a laptop or phone browser, and about an hour.
A person filling in an online form
Your first Zap starts the moment someone submits a form like this.
Step 1: prepare the form and sheet

Create a Google Form with these questions: Full name, Email, Phone, Item ordered, Quantity. In the form's Responses tab, link it to a new Google Sheet. Google then writes every response as a new row, with a Timestamp column first. Do not rename or reorder the header row after you build the Zap; the Zap finds fields by those headers.
Keep the trigger sheet clean

Never type notes, totals or blank rows into the response sheet. If the team needs calculations, make a second tab that reads from the response tab. A tidy trigger sheet prevents most beginner failures.
Step 2: build the Zap
Sign in at zapier.com and choose to create a new Zap.
Trigger: choose Google Sheets and the event 'New Spreadsheet Row'. Connect your Google account through the sign-in window, then pick the spreadsheet and the response worksheet.
Submit one test entry in the form yourself, then click to test the trigger. Zapier should pull in that row with all its fields.
Action: choose Gmail and the event 'Send Email'. Connect Gmail the same way.
Map the fields: 'To' gets the Email field; the subject and body use Full name, Item ordered and Quantity from the trigger.
Test the action. Check your inbox, read the email as a customer would, then publish (turn on) the Zap.

Writing the email
Write the message the business would send by hand, then replace the changing parts with mapped fields. Keep it short and specific, and include what happens next and how to pay or ask questions.
Worked example: a bead shop confirmation Zap
For example, Grace sells bead bags in Port Harcourt and takes orders through a Google Form. She expects about 60 orders a month.
Subject: 'We have your order, ' + Full name.
Body: 'Thank you for ordering ' + Quantity + ' × ' + Item ordered + '. We will send payment details and delivery time on WhatsApp within one working day. Reply to this email if anything is wrong.'
She tests with Quantity 2 and Item ordered 'Mini beaded clutch'. The email reads: 'Thank you for ordering 2 × Mini beaded clutch.'
Usage: 1 action per run, so 60 orders = 60 tasks a month, within the free 100 tasks.
Her sister submits a second test order from her own phone to see the real delay. The email arrives within about 15 minutes, as expected for polling.
Grace's customers now get a confirmation for every order, using about 60 of her 100 free tasks a month, and nobody has to remember to send it.
Never send bank details from an automation you have not locked down

Fraudsters copy business names and send fake account numbers. Keep payment details in one place the owner controls, check every automated message that mentions money, and do not let customer-typed text decide where money is paid. Grace's email deliberately says payment details will come on WhatsApp from her known business number.
Step 3: check Zap history

Open **Zap history** after real orders start. Each run shows whether it succeeded, what data the trigger brought in and what each step sent. Learn to read it now, because it is where you will diagnose every problem later. A run marked as stopped or errored tells you which step failed and why.
Common first-Zap problems
**The trigger finds no new rows.** The test was done before any response existed, or rows were added by hand to a different tab.
**Emails go to the wrong person.** 'To' was typed, not mapped.
**Old responses are emailed.** Turn on the Zap after your test, and check the trigger only picks up new rows; do not paste old data into the response sheet.
**Email lands in spam.** Keep the message plain, avoid all-capital subjects, and send from the business's own Google account rather than a new one.

When you are ready to go beyond two steps, for example adding a row to an order tracker as well as sending the email, you will need a paid plan or a different design. Count tasks first: one more action means one more task per run.

Zapier is simple when every case is handled the same way. Real businesses are rarely like that. Orders inside the city go to one dispatch rider, orders to other states go through a bus park or courier, and the owner wants one summary at the end of the day instead of fifty notifications. Make's visual canvas is built for this kind of branching.
A map with routes between points
A router sends each order down the route that matches its rules, like a dispatcher assigning deliveries.
The scenario you will build

For example, Kemi sells hair products from Lagos. Orders arrive as rows in a Google Sheet with columns Order ID, Customer, Phone, State, Items and Amount. She wants: Lagos orders emailed to her rider; orders from other states copied into an 'Interstate' tab for the courier; and one end-of-day summary for herself.
Kemi's order scenario
Watch new rows (scheduled)
Router splits each order
Lagos: email the rider
Other states: add Interstate row
Daily: aggregate one summary
One trigger feeds a router; each route has a filter, and a separate daily scenario builds the summary.
Building it step by step
In Make, create a new scenario. Add the Google Sheets module 'Watch New Rows' and connect the business Google account. Choose the spreadsheet and sheet, and tell it the table has headers.
Click the trigger's clock to set the schedule. Choose a sensible interval, for example every 2 hours during a trial, and calculate the credits before choosing anything faster.
Add a **Router** after the trigger. A router has no cost in credits and lets one bundle travel down several routes.
On the first route, click the link to set a **filter**: State, text equal to (case insensitive), 'Lagos'. Add a Gmail 'Send an email' module to the rider, mapping Order ID, Customer, Phone and Items.
On the second route, set the filter: State does not equal 'Lagos'. Add a Google Sheets 'Add a Row' module writing to the Interstate tab.
Click 'Run once', add two test rows (one Lagos, one Ogun), and watch the bubbles on each module show how many bundles passed through.
Plan for the cases your filters miss

What if State is blank, or typed 'lagos ' with a space? Use case-insensitive matching, trim spaces, and add a fallback route in Make for anything that matches no rule, so no order silently disappears. A blank State should alert the owner, not vanish.
Iterators and aggregators

Two Make tools change how bundles flow. An **iterator** splits one item that contains a list, such as an email with several attachments, into separate bundles so each can be handled. An **aggregator** does the reverse: it collects many bundles into one. A **Text aggregator** joins them into one block of text, which is perfect for a summary message.
Worked example: counting credits with and without an aggregator
For example, Kemi's separate summary scenario runs once at 8 p.m. and finds 6 orders added that day. She wants them listed in one email to herself.
Without an aggregator: the trigger runs once (1 credit), then the email module runs once per bundle (6 credits). Total 1 + 6 = 7 credits, and Kemi gets 6 emails.
With a Text aggregator: trigger 1 credit + aggregator 1 credit + email 1 credit = 3 credits, and Kemi gets one email listing all 6 orders.
Her main routing scenario, at one check that finds 4 Lagos orders and 2 Ogun orders: trigger 1 + rider emails 4 + Interstate rows 2 = 7 credits. The router itself uses none.
If she later adds a WhatsApp-style alert on the interstate route, that adds 2 more module runs: 7 + 2 = 9 credits for that check.
The aggregator cut the summary from 7 credits and 6 emails to 3 credits and 1 email. Kemi now knows how to estimate the cost of every route before she adds it.
Mapping inside Make

Make shows the fields from earlier modules in a panel when you click into a box. Drag or click them in, exactly as you mapped fields in Zapier. Make also offers functions, for example to format a date or trim spaces, which you place around a field. Keep functions simple and write down what each one does; you will need that note when someone asks why a value looks the way it does.

An automation that works on one clean test row is not finished. Real data is messy: blank fields, phone numbers typed five ways, names with apostrophes, a customer who submits the form twice. Professional work means you find these problems before the client's customers do, and you leave behind a document that lets someone else keep the automation running.
People fixing a bug on a large screen
Testing on purpose with bad data is how you find failures before customers do.
Write a test plan
List the cases you will test, what you expect, and what actually happened. Include at least one normal case, several edge cases and one deliberate failure.

Do not hand over an automation until every box is ticked.
Error handling in Make

Make's documentation lists five error handlers you can attach to a module: **Ignore** (skip the error and continue), **Resume** (continue with a substitute value you provide), **Commit** (keep changes made so far and stop), **Rollback** (undo changes where the apps allow it, and stop) and **Break** (stop and store the run so it can be completed later). Without a handler, Make by default disables a scheduled scenario after 3 errors in a row, and an instantly triggered scenario is disabled immediately when an error happens. You can also switch on storing **incomplete executions** in the scenario settings, so a failed run can be retried instead of lost.
Error alerts in Zapier

In Zapier, failed and halted runs appear in Zap history with the step and message. Check your account's notification settings so error emails reach someone who will act, ideally both you and a named person at the client. For important flows, many builders add a simple daily check: does the number of rows in the sheet match the number of confirmations sent?
Worked example: catching a silent failure
For example, Chidinma built an enrolment scenario for a tutoring centre in Abuja. On the third week, the centre's admin changed her Google password, which can break saved connections.
The scenario's next three scheduled runs fail with a connection error.
Because no error handler was set, Make disables the scenario after the third consecutive error, as its default setting describes.
Chidinma had set error notifications to go to herself and to the admin, Musa. Musa sees the alert the same morning.
She reconnects the Google account, retries the stored incomplete executions, and checks History: 9 enrolments were waiting, and all 9 now process.
She adds a line to the run book: 'If you change the Google password, tell Chidinma or reconnect the account in Make, Connections.'
No parent was missed because the failure reached a person quickly and the failed runs were stored. Without alerts, the scenario could have stayed off for weeks.
Protecting personal data

Automations copy names, phone numbers and emails between apps, so they carry personal data. Nigeria has the **Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023**, overseen by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC), and the NDPC names consent, contract and legal obligation among the lawful bases for processing. You do not need to be a lawyer, but you must build responsibly:
Collect and pass on only the fields each step needs. The rider needs the address and phone, not the customer's payment history.
Build inside the **client's own accounts** where possible. Connect apps through their official sign-in windows; never ask for passwords over WhatsApp.
Turn on two-step verification for the Google, Zapier and Make accounts.
Avoid sending sensitive information, such as health details, through automations unless the client has proper advice and safeguards.
When the project ends, remove your access and delete test data that contains real people's details.
The run book

Write one page in plain language for the owner. Include: what the automation does in one sentence; the trigger and each action; which accounts it uses and who owns them; how to tell it is working (for example, 'check History every Monday'); what to do when an alert arrives; and who to call. Add the date and your name. A business should be able to keep using your work even if you are unavailable.

Automation Consulting: Discovery, Pricing and Winning Clients

You learn to run a discovery session that maps a client's real process, to price a build fairly with the platform subscription kept separate, and to control scope. You finish with honest case studies, a chosen niche and a 90-day plan for paid work.
Discovery: mapping a client's manual process step by step
Run a discovery session using structured questions
Draw an as-is process map with triggers, steps, apps and owners
Check whether the client's apps can connect to Zapier or Make
Agree where a human approval step must stay

Clients often arrive with a solution in mind: 'Can you connect our WhatsApp to everything?'. Your job in discovery is to slow down and understand the **process** first. The best automation is often smaller and different from what the client first asked for, and a clear map protects both of you from misunderstanding later.
Two people in a structured conversation
Discovery is a structured conversation about how the work really happens today.
Who to talk to

Speak to the **owner**, who cares about cost and results, and to the **person who does the work**, who knows the real steps and workarounds. They often describe the process differently. Where the two stories disagree, ask the doer to show you on screen. Sixty minutes watching the work beats three meetings talking about it.
Discovery questions that work
**What starts it?** 'What is the very first thing that tells you this task needs doing?' This finds the trigger.
**Walk me through the last time.** Ask about one real recent case, not 'normally'. People skip steps when they generalise.
**Which apps and accounts?** Write down every tool, who owns the login, and whether it is a free or paid plan.
**How often and how long?** Get rough counts per week and minutes per case, as in your audit.
**What goes wrong?** Missed follow-ups, wrong amounts, duplicate records. Ask for one real example.
**What must a person approve?** Refunds, discounts, anything about money or sensitive information.
**What does done look like?** 'Every parent gets a receipt within the same day' is a measurable goal.
A discovery session in 60 minutes
0-10: goals and success measure
10-30: walk through a real case
30-45: apps, accounts and access
45-55: risks and approvals
55-60: agree next step
A fixed agenda keeps discovery focused and ends with a clear next step.
Drawing the as-is map

After the session, draw the current process as numbered boxes: trigger, each step, who does it, which app, and where data is copied by hand. Mark every hand copy with a star; those are your automation points. Mark every decision with a diamond; those either become filters with clear rules or stay human. Send the map back to the client and ask, 'Is this right?'. Corrections at this stage cost nothing.
Worked example: a school fee receipt process
For example, Mrs Bello is the bursar of a private primary school in Ilorin. Parents pay fees by bank transfer, and she sends receipts by hand. The proprietor wants 'everything automated'.
Trigger found: she checks the school's bank alerts each morning. There is no app trigger yet, because the bank alerts arrive as SMS.
Steps mapped: she matches each payment to a pupil in a Google Sheet (5 minutes), types a receipt in Google Docs (6 minutes) and emails it to the parent (2 minutes).
Volume: about 40 payments a week in the busy first weeks of term, so 40 × (5 + 6 + 2) = 520 minutes, nearly 9 hours a week.
Decision point: matching a payment to the right pupil needs judgement when names differ, so it stays human.

Automation point: once she marks a pupil's row 'Confirmed', a scheduled scenario can search the sheet for rows that are confirmed but not yet marked 'Receipt sent', create each receipt from a Google Docs template, email it to the parent's address in the sheet, and then mark the row 'Receipt sent' so no parent gets two receipts.

Instead of 'everything automated', the agreed scope is: Mrs Bello confirms the match, and the automation produces and sends the receipt. That removes about 8 of the 13 minutes per payment while keeping the judgement step human.
Checking the apps can connect

For every app on the map, search the Zapier and Make app directories and note which triggers and actions exist. If an app is not listed, look for a way round: does it send email notifications, export to Google Sheets, or offer webhooks? Banks and some local platforms may not connect at all; in that case a human step, like Mrs Bello's tick box, becomes the trigger.
From as-is to to-be

Once the client agrees the as-is map, draw a second map, the **to-be** process, showing which steps the automation will take over and which stay with people. Keep the same numbering so the client can compare the two side by side. Under the to-be map, write the one-line automation sentences you learned in Module 1, one per automation. Within one working day of the session, send a short discovery summary: the goal, the two maps, the app checks, the risks you found and your recommended next step. This summary often becomes the first page of your proposal, and it shows the client you listened.
Access without risk

Ask the client to create or keep the accounts in the business's name and to invite you, rather than handing you their personal passwords. Never ask for banking logins or card PINs, and never build automations that move money without a person approving each payment.

Pricing an automation project and writing a proposal with clear scope
Estimate build hours and set a fixed project price
Compare the price with the client's estimated monthly savings
Separate your fee from the client's platform subscription
Write a proposal that prevents scope creep

Automation work has three costs that clients often confuse: **your build fee**, **the platform subscription** (Zapier or Make) and **ongoing care** if they want you to watch it. Keep these separate in every proposal. The platform fee is the client's own bill, paid from the client's own account, so they keep control if you part ways.
A pricing page with plan options
Clear prices with separate lines for build, platform and care avoid surprises.
Estimating your build fee

Most automation builds have a clear scope, so a **fixed project price** usually works better than open hourly billing. Estimate hours for each phase, multiply by your hourly rate, and add a small buffer for the unknown. As you gain experience, keep a record of real hours so your estimates improve.
Phase
What it covers
Typical share of effort
Discovery and mapping
Session, as-is map, app checks
About a fifth
Build
Trigger, actions, routes, formatting
The largest share
Testing
Test plan, edge cases, fixes
Handover
Run book, training call, access clean-up
The smallest share
Worked example: pricing the school receipt automation
For example, Halima is quoting Mrs Bello's school for the receipt automation from the last lesson. Her own rate is about ₦8,000 an hour (her choice, approximate).
Hours: discovery 3 + build 6 + testing 3 + handover 2 = 14 hours.
Value check: the school estimates the automation saves Mrs Bello about 12 hours a month, and values her time at about ₦2,500 an hour. 12 × ₦2,500 = ₦30,000 a month.
Optional care plan: ₦15,000 a month for checking History weekly and fixing breakages, up to 2 hours.
Payback with the care plan: ₦112,000 ÷ (₦30,000 − ₦15,000) is about 7.5 months, before the platform subscription, which the school pays directly in dollars at that month's rate.
Halima presents ₦112,000 for the build and an optional ₦15,000 monthly care plan, shows the payback working, and lists the platform plan separately so the school sees every cost.
Value is a reason, not a formula
Savings help the client see the price is fair. Do not promise savings you have not measured, and do not price only on 'value' if the client cannot see how you reached it. Always show your working.
Three package levels
Care plan: monitoring and fixes
Build: tested automation and run book
Audit: process map and recommendations
Many clients start with a paid audit, move to a build, then keep a care plan; each level stands on the one below.
Setting your hourly rate

Start from what you need to earn, not from what you think others charge. Decide a monthly income target, then estimate how many hours a month you can truly bill, remembering that finding clients, admin and learning take time too. For example, if Halima wants about ₦400,000 a month and expects to bill 50 hours, her rate is ₦400,000 ÷ 50 = ₦8,000 an hour. Review the rate every few months as your speed and case studies improve. Faster delivery is a reason to move towards fixed prices, so that you, not the client, benefit from your growing skill.
What a care plan covers

Apps change, passwords change and businesses grow, so automations need occasional attention. A care plan is an optional monthly fee for a fixed amount of looking after: for example, checking run history every week, fixing broken connections, small wording changes and a short monthly report of runs and failures. State the hours included and what counts as new work. Clients who decline a care plan should still receive the run book, so they can manage on their own or call you for paid fixes.
What the proposal must say
**The problem**, in the client's own words, with the measured hours.
**What will be built**: the trigger, every action, every route, and which apps.
**What is not included**: for example 'WhatsApp messages', 'more than one form', 'changes after sign-off'.
**Assumptions**: 'The school provides an admin Google account; the parent email column is complete.'
**Platform cost**: plan name, approximate dollar price on the date of the proposal, paid by the client.
**Timeline and payment**: for example half to start, half on handover after the test plan passes.
**Change requests**: new work is quoted separately before it starts.
Controlling scope

Scope creep is when small extra requests pile up until a fixed price no longer covers the work. It is normal for clients to have new ideas once they see automation working. Welcome the idea, write it down, and reply with a short change note: what it is, the extra hours and the extra price. Only start after they agree in writing, even on WhatsApp. This keeps the relationship friendly and your income fair.
Getting paid safely

Use traceable payments to your business account and send an invoice for each payment. Do not hand over admin access to accounts you created before the agreed payment, but do make sure the client always owns the main business accounts. Beware of 'clients' who send overpayments and ask for refunds to a different account; this is a common scam.

Case studies, choosing a niche and your 90-day plan for paid work
Write an honest before-and-after case study for an automation you built
Choose a niche based on shared, repeatable processes
Plan 90 days of building, outreach and follow-up with weekly targets
Track your own results instead of relying on guesses

Clients hire automation builders they trust, and trust comes from proof. Your portfolio is not a list of tools you have touched. It is a small set of clear stories: here was the manual process, here is what I built, here is what changed, and here is how it handles problems. Two strong case studies beat ten screenshots.
A portfolio website showing project cards
Each project card should tell a short before-and-after story with real numbers.
The case study structure
**Client and context**: type of business and location, with permission. Use first names or 'a Lagos hair products seller' if they prefer privacy.
**Before**: the manual process and the measured hours from your audit.
**What I built**: the trigger, actions and routes, with a screenshot of the Zap or Make canvas. Blur any customer names, emails and phone numbers.
**An edge case**: one problem you planned for, such as blank fields or a failed connection, and how the build handles it.

**After**: what changed, measured where possible, for example 'confirmations now go out for every order; the assistant spends about 2 hours less a week on copying'. Say clearly when a number is an estimate.
**Client comment**: a short quote only if the client actually said it and agreed you can use it.
Honesty is your brand

Never invent results, clients or quotes. If your first case studies are practice builds, label them 'practice project' and describe what you would measure with a real client. Honest practice work is respected; fake results destroy trust when discovered.
Choosing a niche

A niche is a type of client whose processes repeat from one business to the next. When you build a fee-receipt automation for one school, the second school is faster and your case study speaks directly to them. Good niches have digital tools already, repeated paperwork, and owners who feel the pain of missed follow-ups.
**Schools and tutoring centres**: enrolment forms, fee receipts, parent updates.
**Event planners and caterers**: enquiries, quotes, booking confirmations, supplier lists.
**Training providers**: registrations, payment confirmation, certificates, reminders.
**NGOs and community groups**: volunteer sign-ups, beneficiary registers, donor thank-you emails, with extra care for personal data.

Pick the niche where you have contacts or experience. A woman who has worked in a school office already speaks the language of bursars and proprietors, and that is worth more than knowing the newest feature.
Your 90-day plan
Days 1-30: build two case studies
Days 31-60: contact 32 businesses
Days 61-75: discovery calls and proposals
Days 76-90: deliver, then ask referrals
Build proof first, then reach out steadily, then convert conversations into paid work.
Worked example: a 90-day plan with weekly targets
For example, Blessing, a former school administrator in Enugu, chooses schools and tutoring centres as her niche.
Days 1 to 30: she builds the receipt automation for her former school as a free pilot with written permission, and a registration Zap for a tutoring centre, and writes both case studies.
Days 31 to 60: she aims to contact 32 schools and centres, which is 32 ÷ 4 = 8 a week, by visiting, WhatsApp introductions from people she knows, and a short email with one case study attached.
She tracks every contact in a sheet: date, name, response, next step. She does not assume any response rate; she measures her own.
Days 61 to 75: she runs discovery sessions with everyone who replies with interest and sends a proposal within two working days of each one.
Days 76 to 90: she delivers any signed project, writes it up as a third case study, and asks each happy client for one introduction.
By day 90 Blessing has two or three case studies, a contact sheet showing her real reply and conversion rates, and a pipeline she can grow. Her next 90 days are planned from her own numbers.
A short outreach message
Your first message should be short, specific to the niche and about their problem, not about tools. Keep it to a few sentences and attach or link one case study.
Open with the pain: 'Many schools spend hours each week typing fee receipts by hand.'
Show proof: 'For a primary school in Ilorin, I set up receipts that are created and emailed once the bursar confirms a payment.'
Make a small offer: 'I can map your receipt process in a free 30-minute call and show you what could be automated.'
Close politely with your name, phone number and business email.
Follow up once after about a week if there is no reply, then stop. Record every follow-up in your tracking sheet so you never message the same person twice by mistake.
Keep learning, carefully

Both Zapier and Make publish help centres and learning material on their own websites, and both add features often. Spend an hour a week reading the official help pages for the features you use, and re-check plan limits before each proposal. As you grow, you may add a second platform or learn webhooks in more depth, but master one niche and one platform first.

Zapier and Make move information from one app to another and act on it, the same way every time, without anyone pressing buttons.
They are not magic. If the work is messy, automation copies the mess faster. So your first skill is seeing the work clearly.
In this module you will learn to measure how many hours a task costs.
And how each platform counts usage, so you can predict the monthly cost.
Four tests
Is this task a good candidate?
It repeats many times a week
It follows clear rules: when X happens, do Y
The data is already digital
Mistakes cost something
Learn these four tests by heart. First, the task repeats. It happens many times a week, not twice a year.
Second, it follows clear rules. You can write it as, when X happens, do Y. If the rule is, it depends on how I feel, it is not ready.
Third, the data is already digital, in a form, a spreadsheet or an email. Paper records must be typed first, and Zapier or Make cannot do that typing for you.
Fourth, mistakes cost something. A missed follow-up loses a sale.
Judgement calls, like refunds or angry complaints, stay with a person. Automation only gathers the facts and alerts her.

Shared language
How every automation runs
Trigger: the event that starts it
Map fields from the trigger. Never type fixed values.
Zapier and Make think the same way. A trigger is the event that starts the automation, such as a new form response. Each automation has one trigger.
A filter checks a rule and stops runs that should not continue.
Then an action does the work, like sending an email. In it you map fields. You do not type a name into the email. You insert the Name field, so each run uses its own name.
Every run is saved in history to check later.
Typing a fixed value where a field should go is the most common beginner mistake. Every customer then gets the same name or amount.
Counting usage
How each platform counts
Zapier: tasks
One task per successful action
Triggers never use tasks
Filters and Formatter are free
Free plan: 100 tasks
Make: credits
One credit per module run
Each scheduled check counts
Runs once per bundle
Free plan: 1,000 credits
Zapier counts tasks. A task is any successful action. Triggers, filters and Formatter steps do not use tasks. The free plan gives 100 tasks a month, at the time of writing.
Make counts credits. Each module run is one credit by default, including every time a scheduled trigger checks for new data, even on quiet days.
The free plan gives 1,000 credits. So the schedule you choose changes the bill.

A safety point about money. Fraudsters copy business names and send fake account numbers. So keep payment details in one place the owner controls, and check every automated message that mentions money.

Branching in Make
Kemi's order router
Watch New Rows, on a schedule
Router after the trigger
Lagos route: email the rider
Other states: add an Interstate row
Fallback route for anything else
Add a fallback route so no order silently disappears.
For example, Kemi sells hair products from Lagos. In Make, the trigger watches her order sheet for new rows. During a trial, a check every 2 hours is sensible.
Next comes a router. It uses no credits and lets each order travel down different routes.
On the first route, a filter lets through State equal to Lagos, and Gmail emails the rider.
On the second, State is not Lagos, so a row is added to the Interstate tab for the courier.
What if State is blank, or typed with an extra space? Trim spaces, match without caring about capital letters, and add a fallback route that alerts the owner.
Real data is messy
Three things to test
Blank fields, phone numbers typed different ways, odd names, the same customer submitting twice.
Remove a connection on purpose. Check that the error is recorded and a person is alerted.
In Make, store incomplete executions so a failed run can be retried, not lost.
Test on purpose with bad data. Try blank fields, phone numbers typed different ways, names with apostrophes, and a customer who submits twice.
Test a failure too. Make, by default, switches off a scheduled scenario after 3 errors in a row. So send error alerts to you and to a named person at the client.

For example, Chidinma's enrolment scenario stopped when the admin changed a Google password. Musa saw the alert that morning. She reconnected, retried the stored runs, and all 9 waiting enrolments went through.

Clients often arrive with a solution in mind, like, can you connect our WhatsApp to everything?

Discovery
Questions that find the real process
What starts it?
Walk me through the last time
Which apps and accounts?
What goes wrong?
What must a person approve?
What does done look like?
Talk to the owner and to the person who does the work. Ask, what is the very first thing that tells you this task needs doing? That finds the trigger.
Ask about one real recent case, not what normally happens. People skip steps when they generalise.
Write down every app, who owns the login, and whether it is free or paid.
Ask for one real example of what goes wrong.
Find what a person must approve, like refunds or anything about money.
And agree what done looks like, for example, every parent gets a receipt the same day.

Mrs Bello's fee receipts
Map: match payment, type receipt, email it
About 40 payments a week, nearly 9 hours
Matching needs judgement: stays human
She ticks Confirmed; automation sends receipt
Stars mark hand copies to automate. Diamonds mark decisions.
For example, Mrs Bello is the bursar of a primary school in Ilorin. She matches each bank payment to a pupil, types a receipt, and emails it to the parent.
In busy weeks that is about 40 payments, and 520 minutes, nearly 9 hours a week.
Matching a payment to the right pupil needs judgement when names differ, so it stays human.
Once she marks a row Confirmed, a scenario creates the receipt, emails it, and marks the row Receipt sent, so no parent gets two.
On your map, a star marks each hand copy to automate. A diamond marks each decision, which becomes a clear rule or stays human. Send the map back and ask, is this right?

Scope
Control scope kindly
Do
List what is not included
Write a change note for new ideas
Start only after written agreement
Avoid
Doing small extras for free
Promising unmeasured savings
Starting on a verbal yes
Scope creep is when small extra requests pile up until the fixed price no longer covers the work. So your proposal lists what is not included.
When a new idea comes, welcome it and send a short change note with the extra hours and price. Start only after written agreement, even on WhatsApp.
Avoid doing extras for free, and never promise savings you have not measured.
Safety
Access and payment safety
Accounts stay in the business's name. Ask to be invited. Never take banking logins or card PINs.
Never build automations that move money without a person approving each payment.
Use traceable payments and invoices. Beware overpayments with refunds to a different account.
Stay safe with access. Accounts stay in the business's name, and they invite you. Never ask for banking logins or card PINs.
Never build an automation that moves money without a person approving each payment.
Get paid into your business account with an invoice each time. A client who overpays and asks for a refund to a different account is a common scam.
Your plan
Proof first: a 90-day plan
Days 1 to 30: build two case studies
Days 31 to 60: contact 32 businesses
Days 61 to 75: discovery and proposals
Days 76 to 90: deliver, ask for referrals
Never invent results, clients or quotes.
For example, Blessing, a former school administrator in Enugu, picks schools as her niche. In the first 30 days she builds two case studies: before, what she built, one edge case, and after.
Then she contacts 32 schools, 8 a week, and tracks every reply in a sheet.
She runs discovery with everyone interested, and sends a proposal within two working days.
Finally she delivers, writes a third case study, and asks each happy client for one introduction.
Honesty is your brand. Label practice work as a practice project, and blur personal data in screenshots.
